name: Smart Stage Math
tagline: Math, but make it a performance. Take your position. 🩰
howToPlay: Read the problem, then solve it one line at a time. Tap Check! after every line and we'll tell you exactly where it went wrong. Stuck? Grab a hint or tap Show me how.
levelPickerSubtitle: Level 1 = the warm-up barre. Level 5 = opening night. 🌟
footerNote: ✨ No sign-up, no passwords — just you, the numbers, and the curtain call.

levels.name: The Missing Dancers
levels.cheer: Some dancers were already warming up. Then 47 more arrived for the rehearsal, and now there are 132 in the studio. 🩰
levels.question: How many were warming up to begin with?
hints: The x is stuck with a “+ 47”. Get rid of it.
Subtract 47 from BOTH sides to keep it balanced.

walkthrough.title: Find the goal
walkthrough.body: We want x on its own. Right now it has “+ 47” attached.

levels.name: Sheet Music
levels.cheer: The choir has 6 identical music folders. Altogether they hold 84 pages of sheet music. 🎼
levels.question: How many pages are in one folder?
hints: 6x means 6 times x. To undo times, you divide.

levels.name: Costume Budget
levels.tagline: Two moves, in the right order.
levels.cheer: Each costume costs the same. You ordered 3 of them plus a $12 box of ribbon, and spent $45 in total. 🎭
levels.question: How much was one costume?
hints: Deal with the lonely number first. That + 12 goes.

walkthrough.title: Split it up
walkthrough.body: x is multiplied by 3, so divide BOTH sides by 3.

levels.name: Paper Doll Sale
levels.cheer: You had some money saved for paper doll sets. You found $2.75 in your coat pocket, and now you have $9.50. ✂️
levels.question: How much had you saved?
hints: Same idea as before — undo the addition.

walkthrough.title: Same move, new numbers
walkthrough.body: A decimal changes nothing about the method.

walkthrough.title: Subtract carefully
walkthrough.body: 9.50 − 2.75 = 6.75. Keep the decimal points lined up.

levels.name: Opening Night
levels.cheer: The stage holds 2 identical rows. Each row has your dancers plus the 5 guest performers. Altogether 34 people are on stage. 🎭
levels.question: How many of your dancers are in each row?
hints: You can divide both sides by 2 first, or multiply out the bracket. Either works.

walkthrough.title: Undo the outside first
walkthrough.body: The whole bracket is multiplied by 2, so divide BOTH sides by 2. 34 ÷ 2 = 17.

_themeNote: Red only — one hue throughout, no second brand colour. Correct/wrong feedback keeps green and a darker red, because those must stay readable as signals rather than decoration.

lessons.title: What x actually is
lessons.subtitle: It's just a number wearing a disguise.

teach.heading: x is a hiding place
teach.body: When you don't know a number yet, you give it a letter and carry on. That's all algebra is. If ribbons come in a box and you don't know how many, call it x and keep going.
teach.example: x = the number we don't know yet

teach.heading: It's ONE number, not any number
teach.body: In one problem, x is a single fixed number the whole way through. It doesn't change halfway. Your job is to find out which number it was all along.
teach.example: x + 3 = 7   →   x was 4 the entire time

teach.heading: You can already do this
teach.body: You've been doing it since you were small. “What plus 3 makes 7?” is algebra. Writing x instead of “what” is the only new part.

practice.prompt: You find a sealed box of ribbons. The label says the box plus 5 loose ones makes 12 altogether.
practice.question: If x is what's in the box, which equation says that?
practice.explain: The box (x) AND 5 more makes 12. “And” means add: x + 5 = 12.

practice.prompt: Someone insists x means “any number you like, it's basically vibes.”
practice.question: In the equation x + 2 = 9, how many numbers can x be?
practice.explain: Only 7 works. In one equation, x is one fixed number — not a mood.

practice.prompt: Your dance teacher writes “? × 4 = 20” on the board and then, for no reason, rewrites it.
practice.question: Which rewrite means exactly the same thing?
practice.explain: 4x is shorthand for 4 × x. The ? just became an x.

practice.prompt: You see this written down: y + 1 = 6.
practice.question: Is that still algebra, even though it isn't an x?
practice.explain: The letter is just a label. x, y, n, or a smiley face — it's whatever number is hiding.

reinforce.prompt: A crate of ribbons plus 8 spare ones makes 20.
reinforce.question: Which equation says that?
reinforce.explain: The crate (x) and 8 more, together, is 20. Together means add.

reinforce.prompt: In the equation n − 2 = 10, someone says n could be lots of things.
reinforce.question: How many numbers actually work?
reinforce.explain: Only 12 works. One equation, one hidden number.

reinforce.question: Which one is that in algebra?
reinforce.explain: “Times” means multiply, and 3x is how we write 3 × x.

reinforce.prompt: Two people write the same problem: one uses x, the other uses b.
reinforce.question: Are they doing the same maths?
reinforce.explain: The letter is a name tag, not a rule. Same problem either way.

lessons.title: The balance rule
lessons.subtitle: An equals sign is a promise, not a full stop.

teach.heading: = means the two sides weigh the same
teach.body: Think of an equation as an old-fashioned scale. The equals sign says: this side and that side balance exactly. Not “the answer is next” — balance.
teach.example: x + 3 = 7   →   left side weighs the same as right side

teach.heading: Do it to one side, do it to the other
teach.body: You can change an equation as much as you like, on one condition: whatever you do to one side, you do the identical thing to the other. Then it still balances.

teach.heading: Break the rule and it stops being true
teach.body: Take something off one side only and the scale tips. The equation is now a lie, and everything after it is wrong too. This is the single most common mistake in all of algebra.
teach.example: x + 3 = 7   →   take 3 off the left only   →   x = 7   ✗

practice.prompt: You have 6 = 6. Comforting. True. You subtract 2 from the left side only, because you're feeling reckless.
practice.question: What do you have now?
practice.explain: Touch one side only and it stops balancing. That's why we always do both.

practice.prompt: x + 4 = 9. You want x on its own.
practice.question: What should you do?
practice.explain: The + 4 is stuck to x. Subtract 4 from BOTH sides and it lifts off, still balanced.

practice.prompt: Someone divides the left side of an equation by 2 and leaves the right side alone, then insists the routine is fine.
practice.question: Is the equation still true?
practice.explain: Halving one side and not the other tips the scale. It's false from that line onward.

practice.prompt: 2x = 10, and you multiply BOTH sides by 3 for absolutely no reason.
practice.question: Is the equation still true?
practice.explain: Both sides, same thing — it stays balanced. Useless here, but perfectly legal.

reinforce.prompt: 10 = 10. You add 5 to the right side only.
reinforce.question: What's true now?
reinforce.explain: One side only always breaks it.

reinforce.prompt: x − 6 = 2 and you want x alone.
reinforce.question: What do you do?
reinforce.explain: A − 6 is undone by + 6, on BOTH sides.

reinforce.prompt: 3x = 12, and you divide both sides by 3.
reinforce.question: Still true?
reinforce.explain: Both sides, same operation. Balanced — and now x is alone.

reinforce.prompt: Someone says “the equals sign just means here comes the answer.”
reinforce.question: Are they right?
choices: No — it means both sides are equal
reinforce.correct: No — it means both sides are equal
reinforce.explain: It's a balance, not an arrow. That idea carries you through all of algebra.

lessons.title: Undoing things
lessons.subtitle: Every operation has an opposite that cancels it.

teach.heading: Opposites cancel
teach.body: Adding is undone by subtracting. Multiplying is undone by dividing. To set x free, do the opposite of whatever is stuck to it.

teach.heading: Look at what's attached to x
teach.body: Read the equation and ask one question: what is being done TO x? Then do the opposite of that, to both sides.

teach.heading: 5x means 5 TIMES x
teach.body: When a number sits right against a letter, they're being multiplied. There's no hidden plus. So you undo it by dividing.

practice.prompt: x + 9 = 15 has a clingy + 9 that will not leave the rehearsal room.
practice.question: How do you get rid of it?
practice.explain: Adding is undone by subtracting. x = 6.

practice.question: What's being done to x, and what undoes it?
practice.explain: 7x is 7 × x. Divide both sides by 7 and x = 6.

practice.prompt: x ÷ 3 = 4. Unusual, but it happens.
practice.question: What undoes a divide by 3?
practice.explain: Multiplying undoes dividing. x = 12.

practice.prompt: Someone solves x − 4 = 10 by subtracting 4 from both sides and gets x = 6.
practice.question: What went wrong?
practice.explain: The 4 was being subtracted, so add it back. x = 14, not 6.

reinforce.question: What undoes the + 12?
reinforce.explain: Opposite of adding is subtracting. x = 8.

reinforce.question: What do you do?
reinforce.explain: 9x means 9 × x, so divide. x = 4.

reinforce.question: What undoes the − 7?
reinforce.explain: Subtracting is undone by adding. x = 10.

reinforce.question: What undoes it?
reinforce.explain: Multiplying undoes dividing. x = 30.

teach.heading: One move is all it takes
teach.body: Find what's attached to x. Do the opposite, to both sides. Done. That's the whole method and it never changes.

teach.heading: Always check it
teach.body: Put your answer back into the original and see if it balances. If it does, you're right. This takes five seconds and catches almost every mistake.

practice.prompt: You had some ribbons, were handed 7 more, and now have 19.
practice.question: Solve x + 7 = 19.
practice.explain: Subtract 7 from both sides. 19 − 7 = 12. Check: 12 + 7 = 19 ✓

practice.prompt: 6 equal costumes hold 54 ribbons altogether.
practice.question: Solve 6x = 54.
practice.explain: Divide both sides by 6. 54 ÷ 6 = 9. Check: 6 × 9 = 54 ✓

practice.prompt: You lost 8 ribbons and have 15 left. Tragic, but solvable.
practice.question: Solve x − 8 = 15.
practice.explain: Add 8 to both sides. 15 + 8 = 23. Check: 23 − 8 = 15 ✓

practice.prompt: x = 5 is offered as the solution to x + 5 = 20. Confidently.
practice.question: Is it right?
practice.explain: Checking catches it instantly. x = 15.

reinforce.question: What is x?
reinforce.explain: Subtract 4. Check: 7 + 4 = 11 ✓

reinforce.question: What is x?
reinforce.explain: Divide by 5. Check: 5 × 9 = 45 ✓

reinforce.question: What is x?
reinforce.explain: Add 3. Check: 15 − 3 = 12 ✓

reinforce.question: What is x?
reinforce.explain: Multiply by 2. Check: 16 ÷ 2 = 8 ✓

lessons.title: Two-step equations
lessons.subtitle: Two things stuck to x, and an order to peel them off.

teach.heading: Undo the lonely number first
teach.body: When x has both a multiply AND an add stuck to it, deal with the number standing on its own first. Then deal with the one touching x.

teach.heading: It's the reverse of how you'd build it
teach.body: To build 3x + 4 you'd multiply first, then add. To take it apart you go backwards: undo the add, then undo the multiply. Last on, first off.

teach.heading: Check it the same way
teach.body: Put your answer back into the original, both steps. If it balances, you're finished.

practice.prompt: Costumes cost the same each. You bought 2 and a $5 pair of tights, and spent $17.
practice.question: Solve 2x + 5 = 17.
practice.explain: Subtract 5 → 2x = 12. Divide by 2 → x = 6. Check: 2(6) + 5 = 17 ✓

practice.prompt: Someone divides by 3 FIRST on 3x + 6 = 18, before touching the 6.
practice.question: What's the safe order?
practice.explain: Undo the lonely number first. Dividing first works only if you divide EVERY term — easy to get wrong.

practice.question: What is x?
practice.explain: Add 3 → 4x = 24. Divide by 4 → x = 6. Check: 4(6) − 3 = 21 ✓

practice.prompt: x = 4 is offered for 5x + 2 = 27.
practice.question: Does it check out?
practice.explain: Checking catches it. Subtract 2 → 5x = 25 → x = 5.

reinforce.question: What is x?
reinforce.explain: Subtract 2 → 3x = 12. Divide by 3 → x = 4.

reinforce.question: What is x?
reinforce.explain: Add 6 → 2x = 16. Divide by 2 → x = 8.

reinforce.question: Pick the first step.
reinforce.explain: Lonely number first. Then 5x = 25 → x = 5.

reinforce.question: What is x?
reinforce.explain: Subtract 1 → 6x = 24. Divide by 6 → x = 4.
